extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals, marketers, and business communicators who write press releases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and formatting the dateline of a press release to conform to AP Style — where to place it, what to include (city/state), how to format dates and state abbreviations, and special-case exceptions for major metros.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline placement
rubrics_metrics.description: The dateline is found at the beginning of the press release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the dateline at the start of the release — it’s the first thing a reader and any journalist considering picking up your story will see. Make it immediately visible (often highlighted in examples) because journalists want real, current news, not something weeks out of date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dateline core content (AP Style)
rubrics_metrics.description: AP Style: dateline should contain “a city name, entirely in capital letters, followed in most cases by the name of the state, county, or territory where the city is located.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format the dateline as CITY_NAME (all caps), followed by the state/county/territory when appropriate. Example forms shown: (BOSTON). Using this familiar format demonstrates professionalism and the information journalists need to develop stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large metropolitan exceptions (no state required)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some large metropolitan areas do not require the state in the dateline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include the state for these commonly recognized metros: ATLANTA; BOSTON; CHICAGO; SAN FRANCISCO; SAN DIEGO; WASHINGTON. When in doubt, follow AP’s list of metro exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct AP-style state abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a state is required in the dateline, use the AP Stylebook state abbreviation rather than the postal abbreviation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: KANSAS CITY, Mo. (Missouri); PORTLAND, Ore. (Oregon). Note that AP abbreviations are not the same as postal ones and are not always consistent. Refer to AP lists (e.g., Calif., Colo., Conn., Fla.) for the correct forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: State names never abbreviated in AP Style
rubrics_metrics.description: There are eight state names that are never abbreviated in AP Style even if accompanied by a city name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never abbreviate these states in a dateline: Alaska; Hawaii; Idaho; Iowa; Maine; Ohio; Texas; Utah. Write them out in full per AP guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date formatting (numerals and month names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dates should use Arabic numerals without ordinal indicators (no st, nd, rd, th). Months should be capitalized and spelled out when used alone or with the year; when used with a specific date, certain months are abbreviated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use forms like Jan. 31, 2022. Use only Jan., Feb., Aug., Sept., Oct., Nov., and Dec. as abbreviations with specific dates. When a phrase lists only a month and year, do not separate with commas (e.g., January 2022). When listing month, date, and year, separate the year with a comma (e.g., Jan. 31, 2022). Because online content persists, include the year to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma and punctuation rules for dates in datelines
rubrics_metrics.description: When a month is used with a specific date and year, the year should be separated by a comma; month+year phrases do not need a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct examples: Jan. 31, 2022 (BOSTON). Example contrasting forms in article: Jan. 7, 2022– BOSTON and Jan. 7, BOSTON; follow AP’s comma rules and punctuation spacing consistently in the dateline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer AP Style for press release credibility and pickup
rubrics_metrics.description: Using AP Style in your press release dateline and overall format increases the chance media will gravitate to your story and demonstrates professionalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhering to AP wording and format shows an understanding of the information journalists need and presents your release in a familiar standardized format, improving the likelihood of media pickup.
